introduction: The readings ask for more than goodwill: unity of thought, of belief and of purpose, reached by consulting without insisting on one's own view and kept by gathering around one Law and one centre. The later readings, from letters of guidance, ask believers to abide by the decision of their elected Assembly even when it may be mistaken, and to drop the names of party. Scripture and the classics supply many voices for concord, from the Psalms and Paul to the Rig Veda, Cyprian and Lincoln. Because the guide asks so much, it is also read here with those who feared agreement bought at the cost of truth or conscience: Socrates and the apostles before their judges, Milton, Mill, Thoreau, Emerson and Madison.
questions: One reading says that to unite on a matter and be wrong is better than to differ and be right. What reasons do the readings give, and how do Mill and Socrates answer?
What distinguishes the consultation these readings describe from a debate in which truth and falsehood grapple?
The letters ask for obedience to an Assembly that may be mistaken, and say a wrong decision will be set right. By what means do the readings expect that to happen?
Which differences do the readings want gathered under one word, and which do they leave free?
Where would you draw the line Aristotle draws between harmony and unison?

outside.why: Saxe's blind men dispute loud and long, each stiff in his own opinion, each partly in the right and all in the wrong.
Proverbs holds that where there is no counsel the people fall, and that safety lies in a multitude of counsellors.
Paul asks that nothing be done through strife or vainglory, each esteeming the other better than himself.
Paul asks the Philippians to complete his joy by being likeminded, having the same love and being of one accord.
Amos asks the plain question behind the reading: can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Mill holds that all mankind would not be justified in silencing one dissenter, since he may be right. Can agreement on what is wrong ever be better than a difference in which someone is right?
Socrates tells the Athenians that he honours and loves them but will obey God rather than them. Is there a point at which being right matters more than being united?
Jesus promises to be in the midst wherever two or three are gathered together in his name.
Acts remembers the first believers as a multitude of one heart and of one soul.
An Indian teacher pictures rivers that run east and west in their own beds and become the one sea.
The Preacher holds that two are better than one, for they have a good reward for their labour.
Paul's figure for many working as one is the body, one though it has many members.
Jesus gives love for one another as his new commandment and the mark of his disciples.
The Qur’an invites the people of earlier scriptures to come to a word common between them, the worship of God alone.
Gandhi held that the need of the moment is not one religion but mutual respect and tolerance among the devotees of different religions. Is one common Faith the only remedy for a divided world?
The Qur’an says that God could have made mankind one community but tries them in what he has given, so they should vie in good works. Why might the many ways be left to stand?
The psalm exclaims how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
A disciple of Confucius says that for the respectful and courteous man all within the four seas are brothers.
Paul beseeches the Corinthians to speak the same thing and be perfectly joined together in the same mind.
Milton holds that where there is much desire to learn there will be much arguing and many opinions. Is unity of opinion the aim of a living community, or a sign that learning has stopped?
Tennyson imagined such a gathering as a parliament of man, a federation of the world.
Zamenhof, the maker of Esperanto, held that difference of speech is a cause of antipathy, even of hatred, between peoples.
In Genesis the people are one and have all one language, and nothing they imagine will be restrained from them. Is one tongue a blessing to be recovered, or a power the story is wary of?
The Great Learning traces the order of the state back to the cultivation of each person.
Mill calls a general State education a contrivance for moulding people to be exactly like one another. How is directing public thought to a single point to be kept from that?
Isaiah foresees all peoples made joyful together in one house of prayer.
Paul says of Christ that he made both one and broke down the middle wall of partition between peoples.
Acts says that at Pentecost the disciples were all with one accord in one place.
Hebrews asks believers not to forget to entertain strangers, for some have entertained angels unawares.
The Qur’an says that all the wealth of the earth could not have attuned those hearts, but God attuned them.
Jesus prays that his followers may all be one, a unity others are meant to see.
John sees a multitude no man could number, of all nations, kindreds, peoples and tongues, before one throne.
Gibran asks those who love to stand together yet not too near, like the pillars of a temple. How much sameness does concord need?
John's letter says that one who claims to love God and hates his brother is a liar.
Paul wants no schism in the body, its members having the same care one for another.
Proverbs says that hatred stirs up strifes, but love covers all sins.
Cyprian uses the reading's figures: many rays and one light, many branches and one root, many streams and one spring.
Jesus speaks of sheep not yet of this fold who shall be brought, so that there is one fold and one shepherd.
Paul writes to friends he cannot see that though absent in the flesh he is with them in the spirit.
Swift observed that we have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.
The Qur’an bids believers hold fast, all together, to the cable of God, and not separate.
Emerson calls society a joint-stock company whose members agree to surrender liberty for security. What keeps a gathering where all are of one thought from being that?
A hymn of the Rig Veda bids the assembly speak together and let their minds be of one accord.
Isaiah foresees nations beating swords into plowshares and learning war no more.
The Qur’an itself warns against those who split up their religion into sects, each exulting in its own tenets.
Madison found the security of religious rights in the multiplicity of sects. Is the division of a religious community only weakness, or also a protection?
Lincoln took up the saying that a house divided against itself cannot stand.
Jeremiah's tree planted by the waters spreads out its roots and is not anxious when heat comes.
Yeats gives the fear behind the reading in a line: things fall apart, the centre cannot hold.
Bacon counted heresies and schisms the greatest of scandals, worse even than corruption of manners.
Paul asks his readers to endeavour to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Paul tells Titus to avoid contentions and strivings about the law as unprofitable and vain.
Paul asks the Romans to mark those who cause divisions contrary to what they have learned, and to avoid them.
Pope lets the world disagree in faith and hope and asks agreement only in charity. Is one Law needed for unity, or would charity be enough?
Jefferson told a divided country that every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle.
Peter asks believers to be all of one mind, having compassion one of another and loving as brethren.
The Qur’an says of earlier peoples that they broke their religion into sects, each group rejoicing in its tenets.
The Buddha says of teachers who quarrel and fight that they are people seeing one side.
Mill holds that he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that.
Proverbs says that iron sharpens iron, and so a man sharpens the countenance of his friend.
Milton would let truth and falsehood grapple, for who ever knew truth put to the worse in a free and open encounter?
The Laws tell Socrates that a citizen must do what his city orders, or else change its view of what is just.
The apostles tell the council that they ought to obey God rather than men. When a body may be wrong, what tells obedience for unity's sake from obedience against conscience?
Tennyson's soldiers were not to reason why, only to do and die. What separates learning to obey a mistaken decision from that kind of obedience?
Paul asks believers to be subject to those in authority, to speak evil of no man and to be no brawlers.
Thoreau asks why every man has a conscience if he must resign it to the legislator, and would be a man first. What becomes of conscience when abiding by a mistaken decision is the lesser harm?
Shakespeare's king says every subject's duty is the king's, but every subject's soul is his own. What does one who follows an order he doubts keep for himself?
Mill warns that even a true opinion, if not fully and fearlessly discussed, is held as a dead dogma. If a decision is accepted without further dispute, how is a wrong one found out?
Emerson says, trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. What is lost and what is gained when a believer sets his own view aside?
Isaiah has God himself say, come now, and let us reason together.
Acts calls the Bereans noble because they received the word readily and searched the scriptures daily to see whether it was so.
Aristotle holds that he who bids the law rule bids God and reason rule, while the rule of a man adds an element of the beast.

Washington allows that parties in free countries may, within certain limits, serve as checks and keep alive the spirit of liberty. What does a community with no liberals and conservatives use for a check?
The Buddha describes one who abandons divisive speech and does not carry tales that break people apart, but delights in concord.
Aristotle wants unity in family and state but not in all things, lest harmony pass into unison. What differences must unity keep if it is the alpha and omega?
